lead: Castigliano's theorem turns a strain energy formula into a deflection. Write the strain energy U of a linear elastic body as a function of an applied load P, differentiate with respect to P, and the result is the displacement Δ at that load, along that load. It is the quickest route to the deflection of a beam, a frame or a truss once the strain energy is written down.
prereq: You need strain energy in axial, bending and torsion loading for U = P²L/(2AE), U = ∫M²/(2EI) dx and U = T²L/(2GJ).

sections.h3: Why the slope of U is a deflection

blocks.text: For a linear elastic body, ∂U/∂P = Δ at the load P, along P; ∂U/∂M = θ. This is Castigliano's second theorem.

blocks.where: U is strain energy (J); P is load (N); Δ is displacement (m) along P; M is moment (N·m); θ is rotation (rad).

blocks.text: Load and deflection grow together, so U = ½PΔ. For an axial member, U = P²L/(2AE), so dU/dP = PL/(AE) = Δ.
An aluminium strut has L = 1.2 m, A = 250 mm², E = 70 GPa. With P in kN, U = 0.03429 P² J. At P = 20 kN, dU/dP = 0.06857 P = 1.371 J/kN, which is 1.371 mm. Directly, Δ = PL/(AE) = 1.371 × 10⁻³ m.
Read backwards, ∂U/∂Δ = P, Castigliano's first theorem.

sections.h3: The dummy load where no load acts

blocks.text: The theorem needs a load where you want the deflection. Usually there is none, so invent one.

items: Apply a fictitious load Q at that point, along the wanted deflection. For rotation, use a fictitious moment Q.
Write U with Q kept as a symbol.

blocks.text: Set Q = 0 inside U first, and ∂U/∂Q = 0.

A reaction acts at a support; ∂U/∂R gives the support's own movement, zero on a rigid support. Used the other way round, ∂U/∂R = 0 is the compatibility equation that finds a redundant reaction R. For deflections, differentiate real loads or a dummy load at a free point.

sections.h3: Differentiate first, then integrate or sum

blocks.text: Writing U in full and then differentiating is slow. Differentiate under the integral sign instead. Each member or each slice of beam gives its own term.
Δ = Σ N (∂N/∂P) L/(AE)        Δ = ∫ M (∂M/∂P) dx/(EI)
blocks.where: N is the member force and ∂N/∂P its rate of change with the load P; M is the bending moment at x and ∂M/∂P its rate of change with P; L, A, E, I as before.

items: For a truss, ∂N/∂P is the member force caused by a load of 1 at the point, so the sum is exactly the unit load sum of the next chapter.
For a beam, ∂M/∂P is the moment caused by a load of 1 at the point, the m(x) of the unit load method.
With a dummy load Q, write M = M₀ + Qm, so ∂M/∂Q = m; then set Q = 0 and Δ = ∫ M₀ m dx/(EI).

figure.caption: Strain energy of the 1.2 m aluminium strut (A = 250 mm², E = 70 GPa) rises as P². The tangent at 20 kN climbs 6.86 J over 5 kN, a slope of 1.371 J/kN, which is the 1.371 mm extension: Castigliano’s Δ = ∂U/∂P.

examples.question: A steel cantilever is 2 m long, E = 200 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, tip load P = 1 kN. Find U(P) and tip deflection.
steps: Measure x from the free end, so M = Px and U = ∫₀ᴸ P²x² dx/(2EI) = P²L³/(6EI).
6EI = 6 × 200 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ = 9.6 × 10⁶ N·m², and L³ = 8 m³, so U = 8P²/(9.6 × 10⁶) = 8.333 × 10⁻⁷ P² J with P in newtons. At P = 1000 N, U = 0.833 J.
examples.answer: U = 8.333 × 10⁻⁷ P² J (P in N), 0.833 J at 1 kN; tip deflection 1.667 mm downward.

examples.question: A stepped steel bar has E = 200 GPa and pull P = 50 kN. Segment 1: 0.4 m, 400 mm²; segment 2: 0.6 m, 200 mm². Find the extension.
steps: Each segment carries the full pull, so U = P²L₁/(2A₁E) + P²L₂/(2A₂E).
Δ = ∂U/∂P = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ P m = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ × 50 000 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m = 1.0 mm. The thin segment gives 0.75 mm of it.

examples.question: A cantilever of length L = 3 m carries a uniformly distributed load w = 4 kN/m over its whole length; EI = 2400 kN·m². No load acts at the free end. Find the free-end deflection and the free-end rotation by Castigliano’s theorem with a dummy load and a dummy moment.
steps: Put a dummy downward load Q at the free end. Measure x from the free end: M = wx²/2 + Qx (hogging taken positive here), so ∂M/∂Q = x.
Δ = ∫₀ᴸ M (∂M/∂Q) dx/(EI), then Q = 0: Δ = ∫₀³ (wx²/2)(x) dx/(EI) = wL⁴/(8EI).
For rotation put a dummy moment C at the free end: M = wx²/2 + C, so ∂M/∂C = 1. With C = 0, θ = ∫₀³ (wx²/2) dx/(EI) = wL³/(6EI).
examples.answer: Free-end deflection 16.875 mm downward and rotation 0.0075 rad; Q and C were set to zero only after differentiating.

traps: Differentiating with respect to a reaction. It returns the support's own movement, zero on a rigid support; ∂U/∂R = 0 finds a redundant reaction.
Unit slips: J/N is m; J/kN is mm.
dU/dP of P²L/(2AE) is PL/(AE), never PL/(2AE).
Using U = ½PΔ with a deflection from a different load case.

quiz.q: State Castigliano's second theorem for P and for M.

quiz.a: U = ½PΔ grows as P², so dU/dP = PL/(AE) = Δ, a length.

quiz.q: Bar: L = 3 m, A = 300 mm², E = 200 GPa, P = 30 kN. Find U and Δ.
What do you apply where no external load acts?
quiz.a: A fictitious load Q, or a fictitious moment for rotation; set Q = 0 after differentiating.

quiz.q: When does the dummy load become zero? What if earlier?
quiz.a: After differentiation. Earlier, U is constant in Q and ∂U/∂Q = 0.

quiz.q: Two structures carry the same load P plus other loads and store the same total U. Must their deflection at P be equal?
quiz.a: No. With several loads U = ½ΣPᵢΔᵢ, so the same total can be shared differently among the loads, and ½PΔ<sub>P</sub> is not fixed by U. Only when P acts alone does equal U force equal deflection, Δ = 2U/P.

quiz.q: Why does the theorem fail for a nonlinear rubber cord?
quiz.a: The proof uses U = ½PΔ, true only when Δ ∝ P; then ∂U/∂P is not the deflection.

quiz.q: Use Castigliano’s theorem on the two-bar truss of the unit load chapter (each bar 1.8028 m long, sin of its angle with the horizontal 0.8321, AE = 1.4 × 10⁷ N, 10 kN at the apex) to find the apex deflection.

beyond: Not for the exam. For many loads, ∂U/∂Pᵢ = Δᵢ gives the flexibility matrix, used in stiffness and finite element work. Aircraft flexibility methods use it for redundant frames and wing influence coefficients. The dummy-load route and the unit load method end in the same integrals.
